statement: A jacket is reduced by 30%. At the till, a further 10% is taken off the reduced price, and the shopper pays 63 euros. What was the original price?

choices.misconception: I added the two discounts to make 40% off and divided 63 by 0.6.
I only undid the 30% reduction, dividing 63 by 0.7.
I only undid the 10% reduction, dividing 63 by 0.9.
I added 40% of 63 back on, instead of dividing by the fraction of the price that was paid.

hints: The second discount is taken from the reduced price, not the original.
Each discount multiplies the price: 30% off means paying 0.7 of it, then 10% off means paying 0.9 of that. Work out the combined multiplier, then undo it.
The shopper pays $0.7 \times 0.9 = 0.63$ of the original price.

solutions.reliable: After both discounts the shopper pays $0.7 \times 0.9 = 0.63$ of the original price $P$. So $0.63P = 63$, giving $P = 100$ euros. The transferable idea: successive percentage changes multiply, and undoing a change means dividing by its multiplier.
solutions.elegant: Check by going forwards from a choice: 100 euros minus 30% is 70 euros, and 10% off 70 euros leaves 63 euros. The transferable idea: back-solving from a choice confirms a chain of percentages quickly.

whyOnTest: Stacked discounts multiply rather than add, and undoing a percentage means dividing; both traps are on offer here.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
